description:
List every block type this build can place in a model, with a one-line
summary and its required parameters.

Use this FIRST when you are about to build a model and do not yet know the
vocabulary. The `type` strings it returns are exactly what `add_block`
expects. Plugin block types appear here automatically.

`multi_output` marks the only types allowed more than one outgoing link (DECIDE, LOGIC):
every other block may have at most one.
name: list_block_types

description:
Describe one block type: what it does and every parameter with its type,
default and meaning.

Use this before `add_block`/`update_block` whenever you are unsure which
params a type takes -- passing an unknown key is an error, and the defaults
tell you what you may safely leave out. Each description is its first
sentence unless `detail` is true.

detail.description: Every description in full; by default each is its first sentence.

name: describe_block_type

description:
List the distribution names available for a duration or a random draw.

Pass `block_type` (CREATE, DELAY, PROCESS, ...) to get only the ones that
block is usually given; omit it for everything, including plugin entries.
The names are what goes in a block's `distribution` param, a link delay, or
a failure's uptime/downtime.

`summary` is one plain sentence on when to use it. Call describe_distribution for parameter
meanings.

block_type.description: Optional block type (e.g. "CREATE", "DELAY") to list only the distributions offered for it; omit for the whole catalogue.

name: list_distributions

description:
Describe one distribution: when to use it and what each parameter means.

Use it when choosing between, say, Exponential and Lognormal for a service
time, or when you need the exact parameter names for `dist_params`. Every
numeric parameter also accepts an expression string, so a rate may depend
on an entity attribute.
name: describe_distribution

description:
Explain the expression language used by ASSIGN, DECIDE/HOLD conditions,
RECORD, ranking expressions and expression-valued distribution parameters.

Read this before writing any expression: it is a restricted-Python subset
(an AST allow-list, never eval), so anything not listed here is refused at
validation time rather than at run time.
name: get_expression_help

description:
Create an empty model in the workspace under *name*.

This is the starting point for building a model from a description: create
it, add blocks, connect them, then validate. Nothing is written to disk
until you call `save_model`. An empty model validates and runs, and
answers nothing: the first problems appear with the first block.

name.description: Workspace name for the new model (your handle for it later).

name: new_model

description:
Load a model file from the workspace root into the workspace.

Use it to inspect, modify or run an existing model, including the bundled
examples once they have been copied into the root. Older schema versions
migrate on load, so what you get back is always the current format.

name.description: Workspace name to load it under; defaults to the file stem.

path.description: Model .json path, relative to the workspace root.

name: open_model

description:
Draft a model from an event log (a CSV or .xlsx of timestamps per case): what happened
to each case, activity by activity.

The log needs a case id, an activity and a timestamp (or start and end) per row, or XES
traces; lifecycle and resource columns make the draft better. An .xlsx gives cell values,
never formulas; another format is refused. The draft has one CREATE fitted to the case arrivals, one block per activity with its fitted
time, routing from the observed transitions and resources from the resource column,
and opens in the workspace under *name* like `open_model`. Nothing is written to disk.

It is a first draft: read `assumptions` (what the log could not tell) and `dropped`
before trusting its numbers.
The file must be under the workspace root; a log over a size ceiling or with a DOCTYPE
is refused outright, and no argument changes either.

With *idle_waits*, "idle_waits" lists the activities that got a modelled wait. The two lists
are cut to fit one reply; the totals count them all.

columns.description: Headers by role, e.g. {"case": "Patient", "start": "Start time"}; roles: case, activity, timestamp, lifecycle, resource, start, complete; the rest by usual names.

idle_waits.description: true: an activity that waits long at mostly idle resources gets a DELAY fitted to its waits (a modelled wait, not a queue).

name.description: Name for the draft; default the file stem.

path.description: Event log (CSV, .xlsx or .xes), relative to the workspace root.

routing.description: "auto" (a test on the log picks), "markov" (chances to the next activity) or "variants" (one routing per observed sequence).

sheet.description: An .xlsx log's sheet; default the first.

time_unit.description: The draft's time unit: seconds, minutes, hours or days. A numeric timestamp is taken as already in it.

name: import_event_log

description:
Write a model in the workspace to disk as JSON.

Call it once the model validates. A model created with `new_model` has no
path of its own, so the first save needs one.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to save.

path.description: Destination path under the workspace root; defaults to where it was opened.

name: save_model

description:
List the models currently open in the workspace, and the model files
available under the workspace root.

Use it to find out what you can `open_model` and which handles `get_model_summary`
and `run_model` accept.
name: list_models

description:
A compact picture of a model: its blocks with their key parameters, its
links in branch order, its resources, and how many problems it has.

This is the tool to call before editing an existing model, and after a
batch of edits to check the shape is what you intended. It is deliberately
much smaller than `get_model_json`; reach for that only when you need every
field.

Each link is "source -> target"; the ORDER of a block's outgoing links is its branch order
(branch 0 first). "next_options" is what could be done next, at most 3, ranked, each
{"kind", "title", "why", "tool", "arguments", "cost"} (plus "needs": arguments still to
fill in), from the last run's law warnings and what this session has run: offer them, never
run one unasked.
name: get_model_summary

description:
The complete model layout as the JSON that would be saved to disk.

Use it only when `get_model_summary` is not enough -- a full layout is
large. It is also what you would hand to another tool that speaks the model
file format (see the `naga://reference/schema` resource).
name: get_model_json

description:
Add one block to a model and optionally set its parameters in the same
step (one undo entry).

The normal way to build a model: add CREATE, the processing blocks, and
DISPOSE, then `connect` them. Position is cosmetic -- call `auto_layout`
once at the end instead of placing blocks by hand.

A wrong param name or type comes back in "introduced" with code E_PARAM_UNKNOWN /
E_PARAM_TYPE and a hint listing the params this type takes.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Block name; auto-generated (create_1, process_2, ...) when omitted.

params.description: Parameter values to set on the block; the type's defaults fill the rest.

position.description: [x, y] canvas centre in scene units; auto-placed in a row when omitted.

name: add_block

description:
Change an existing block: merge parameters, rename it, move it, or
relabel it -- all as one undo entry.

`params` MERGES rather than replaces, so you can set one value without
restating the rest. Renaming rewires every link automatically.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Current name of the block to change.

new_name.description: Rename the block to this; every link follows the rename.

params.description: Parameters to merge into the block's existing params.

name: update_block

description:
Delete blocks and every link touching them, as one undo entry.

Unknown names are ignored rather than refused, so removing an already-gone
block is not an error. Expect new problems if you cut the flow in half --
the answer says which.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

names.description: Block names to delete; their links go with them.

name: remove_blocks

description:
Link two blocks so entities flow from *source* to *target*, optionally
with a transfer delay.

Links are ORDERED: the n-th link you add out of a DECIDE is its branch n,
matching `probs[n]` / `conditions[n]`. Add branches in the order you want
them, or fix the order afterwards with `reorder_branches`. Only DECIDE and
LOGIC may have more than one outgoing link.

A branching block may send TWO branches to the same target (a DECIDE where
two cases end the same way): the second call returns `index` 1, which
`disconnect` takes to tell them apart.

capacity.description: Parts a link with a delay holds at once (a full link holds its feeder); 0 = no limit.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

source.description: Name of the block the entity leaves.

source_port.description: Out port name: a SUBMODEL instance's port, or a CONVEYOR's exit ("out", "d<k>").

target.description: Name of the block the entity arrives at.

target_port.description: In port name: a SUBMODEL instance's port, or a CONVEYOR's "in".

name: connect

description:
Remove one link. A link that does not exist is a no-op, not an error.

Use it to rewire a flow -- for example to insert a new block between two
existing ones: disconnect a -> c, then connect a -> b and b -> c.

When several parallel links join the pair, name which one with *index*
(0 is the first); leaving it out is then an error listing the candidates.

index.description: Which of several parallel links between the pair, 0 first; only needed when there is more than one.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

source.description: Source block of the link to remove.

target.description: Target block of the link to remove.

name: disconnect

description:
Set the branch order of a block's outgoing links.

Branch order is what binds a DECIDE's `probs[n]` / `conditions[n]` to a
target, so getting it wrong sends entities down the wrong path without any
validation error. *order* must list exactly the current targets of *source*,
permuted.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

order.description: Its target block names in the branch order you want, branch 0 first.

source.description: The branching block (a DECIDE or LOGIC).

name: reorder_branches

description:
REPLACE the model's whole resource table.

For one resource, `upsert_record`; this one sets several at once, or
deletes one by leaving it out. A block's `resource_name` may name a resource or a resource set --
they share one namespace.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

resources.description: The complete resource list, each {"name", "capacity", "discipline", cost fields...}.

name: set_resources

description:
The JSON Schema of one record of *section*: what `upsert_record` expects.

The same `$defs/<item>` the model-file schema uses (MCP resource
naga://reference/schema), with the `$defs` it references. Read it once
before writing the first record of a section.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: get_record_schema

description:
List every record of one section of the model, as stored.

Record sections: resources, resource_sets, schedules, failures, tables,
sequences, variables, entities, timeseries_inputs, levels, flows,
conversions, fixed_costs, fleets, motion_profiles, robots, pallet_patterns, zones,
chargers, auxiliaries, delays, subscripts, agent_types, populations, reality_checks and orders
(keyed by "id"; every other section by "name"). Record shape: schema
$defs/<item>, see get_record_schema.

Sequences are the routings: the operation order a product follows through the
stations (a ROUTE block sends an entity whose `sequence` attribute names one to
each step's STATION); the answer adds "stations", the model's STATION blocks.
Orders are released jobs with a due date ("make `quantity` of `entity_type` on
routing `sequence`, released at `release`, due at `due`", base time unit); the
answer adds "releases", the CREATE blocks in Orders mode. Read them before
writing a sequence or an order name anywhere else.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: list_records

description:
Add one record to a section (a resource, schedule, failure, table, ...), or REPLACE the
one with the same key.

The record is stored as given (record shape: schema $defs/<item>, see
get_record_schema) and the answer reports the validation problems the edit
introduced or fixed -- a missing field, a wrong type, a reference to
something undeclared. To change one field, list_records, edit, upsert.

Typical first records: a "resources" entry {"name", "capacity"} for a
PROCESS/SEIZE to seize; a "variables" entry {"name", "initial"} before an
expression reads it; a "tables" entry for TABLE("name", k); a "levels" and
a "flows" entry for continuous quantities. An agent type's `python` cannot
be written here: code needs the human's consent.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

record.description: The whole record, shaped as get_record_schema(section) says; its key field ("name", or "id" for orders) picks the record to replace.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: upsert_record

description:
Delete one record. References to it elsewhere (TABLE("name"), a flow's
"from", a block's resource_name, ...) come back as problems in the answer,
so fix them in the same batch.

key.description: The record's key: its "name" (its "id" for orders).

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

section.description: Record section, e.g. "resources", "tables", "levels", "agent_types", "orders" (get_record_schema lists them all).

name: remove_record

description:
Give the model REAL DATES, or remove them.

A calendar is optional: without one a model's clock is a plain number in the
base time unit, which is the right choice for an abstract study. Set one
when the study is about real weeks -- weekday shifts, a holiday shutdown, a
tariff or a campaign pinned to dates, or a client report that must say
"Wednesday 10:00". Once set, schedules may be authored as weekday grids,
time series and orders may carry ISO timestamps, and results, charts,
playback and exports all show wall-clock time.

end.description: Optional ISO instant the run ends at, instead of a run-length number.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

start.description: ISO 8601 instant model time 0 stands for, e.g. "2026-01-05T06:00:00". With no offset it is read in `timezone`, never in local time. Pass null to remove the calendar.

timezone.description: IANA name such as UTC or Europe/Rome (default UTC). The wall clock weekday schedules and every date label use.

name: set_calendar

description:
Read a CSV under the workspace root into a lookup table.

Two shapes: a 1-D table is `key,value` under a `key,value` header; a 2-D
table is a header row of column keys whose first cell is EMPTY, then one
row per key. The file must be under the workspace root -- a path that
escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.

column_mode.description: Lookup mode for the column keys.

default.description: Value for a missing exact key.

key_mode.description: Lookup mode for the row keys: exact, step or linear.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Table name to create or replace.

path.description: CSV file under the workspace root.

name: upsert_table_from_csv

description:
List the model's time-series inputs, levels and flows in one answer.

A time series is a profile read by TS("name") -- a PV curve, a site load, a
tariff by hour. A level is a continuous quantity with bounds (battery
energy, tank volume, stock on hand), read by LEVEL("name"). A flow moves
quantity between levels at a rate that is an expression, read by
FLOW("name"). Call this before writing any of those expressions.

Auxiliaries (AUX("name")) and delays (DELAY("name")) are the system-dynamics
records that go with them.

Subscripts are the dimensions records run over. Edit any of these with
upsert_record / remove_record.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

name: list_continuous

description:
Read a `time,value` CSV under the workspace root into a time-series input.

The header row is optional. The file must be under the workspace root -- a
path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Series name to create or replace.

path.description: CSV file under the workspace root, two columns: time and value.

time_unit.description: Unit the time column is in.

name: upsert_timeseries_input_from_csv

description:
The model's path network: the nodes assets sit on and the segments
vehicles and walkers drive along, with the shortest-path distance between
every pair of places.

Coordinates are layout coordinates -- metres once the model's background
image declares a scale. Travel time anywhere in the model is
`distance / speed` along this graph, so this is what to read before
reasoning about how long anything takes to move.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

name: get_network

description:
Add a network node, or move the one with this name.

A node is a PLACE: a dock door, an aisle junction, a pick face. Attach a
block to it with the STATION `node` param and travel to and from that
station becomes the shortest path along the segments.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Node name; a STATION's `node` param, a fleet's `home` and DISTANCE("...", ...) all address it by this.

x.description: Layout x coordinate (metres once the background declares a scale).

name: upsert_node

description:
Delete a network node AND the segments that used it (a segment with a
dangling end is not a thing a model can mean). Blocks whose `node` still
names it come back as E_NETWORK_NODE_UNKNOWN problems.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Node to delete; every segment touching it goes with it.

name: remove_node

description:
Add a drivable segment between two nodes, or replace the one already
joining that ordered pair.

capacity.description: How many vehicles may be on it at once (zone control); omit for unlimited. Two-way with capacity 1 can deadlock head-on.

length.description: Length in layout units. Omit for the straight-line distance times the network's length_factor -- set it for a ramp, a curve or a detour.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

speed.description: Optional speed LIMIT on this segment. It changes travel TIME; the route chosen is still the shortest by length.

two_way.description: False makes it one-way from source to target.

name: upsert_segment

description:
Delete one segment. Check `get_network`'s "unreachable" afterwards: a
removal that strands a routing is an E_NETWORK_UNREACHABLE error.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name: remove_segment

description:
Shortest path between two places on the model's network.

The same number `DISTANCE("source", "target")` returns in an expression, so
use it to sanity-check a travel time before writing one: a trip at speed v
takes `distance / v`.

`distance` is null when no path joins them.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to inspect.

source.description: A node, a STATION block or a station alias.

target.description: Where the trip ends, named the same way.

name: get_distance

description:
REPLACE (or extend) the model's orders from a CSV release list.

Columns: `id` (required), then any of release, due, quantity, entity_type,
sequence, priority, source; every other column becomes a free attribute
assigned onto the order's entities. This is the shape an MES work-order
export already has.

The file is read through the same root confinement as every other file
tool: a path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that
widens that.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

path.description: CSV file to read, inside the workspace root.

replace.description: True (default) replaces the whole order book; False merges by id.

name: upsert_orders_from_csv

description:
REPLACE the model's entity-type table.

Entity types name the things flowing through the model (CREATE's `e_type`)
and carry the per-type WIP `holding_cost` used by the cost KPIs. A model
with no declared types still runs: everything is "DEFAULT".

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name: set_entity_types

description:
Set the model's default run settings; only the arguments you pass change.

ALWAYS set a run length for a model that cannot drain on its own -- one with
an endless CREATE (max_arrivals 0), a failure, or a repeating capacity
schedule. Without it a run raises rather than hanging.

currency.description: Cost label only; never enters the arithmetic.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

replications.description: How many independent replications a run does by default.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units; 0/null means "until the model drains". With a calendar you can set an end DATE instead, with set_calendar.

strict_checks.description: true: conveyor floor checks and run guards are errors, not warnings.

time_unit.description: The model's BASE unit: seconds, minutes, hours or days.

warmup.description: Time at which statistics are reset.

name: set_simulation_settings

description:
Turn on the system-dynamics step grid, change it, or remove it (dt null).

Without it a flow rate is re-evaluated only at events, which is exact for
rates that change only then. A rate that reads LEVEL(), FRACTION() or TNOW
-- dL/dt = -k*L, logistic growth, an SIR model -- needs the grid: it is
re-integrated every dt with Euler or RK4, the way Stella and Vensim do.
Static rates are untouched, and events inside a step stay exact.

dt.description: Step of the system-dynamics grid, > 0; null removes the grid.

method.description: euler (Stella/Vensim default) or rk4 (fourth order; no random draws in a dynamic rate).

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

time_unit.description: Unit dt is in: base (the model's own) or seconds/minutes/hours/days.

name: set_sd_settings

description:
Write the Python class a submodel definition runs (its item code), one undo step.

Hooks, each taking item last: on_entry gets entity and returns the output index (0 first);
on_exit gets entity; on_timer; on_state gets variable and value; on_signal gets name.
LOGIC blocks with hook entry or exit inside the definition run the first two, and
item.params holds the instance's arguments.

The code runs only after a person trusts this exact code on their computer, in the
editor's code panel or with `naga trust`. You cannot trust code, and any change to it
needs the person's yes again. Once trusted, your runs and experiments run it.

"problems" lists what to fix in the code or its wiring.

class_name.description: The class in source the item runs, one instance per placed item.

definition.description: Name of the submodel definition whose code this is.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

signals.description: Signal names that trigger on_signal; $name is per instance.

source.description: The whole Python source: a module defining the class.

timer.description: Run on_timer every this many model time units; null for no timer.

watch.description: Model variables whose writes trigger on_state.

name: set_item_code

description:
Lay the model's blocks out left to right in a deterministic layered
arrangement, one undo entry.

Purely cosmetic -- it changes no behaviour and no KPI. Call it once after
building a model so a human opening it in the editor sees a readable
diagram instead of a pile of blocks.
name: auto_layout

description:
Validate a model file (is it valid?) and return every problem with a stable code, a
JSON-pointer path, and a hint saying how to fix it.

Call this after each batch of edits and ALWAYS before running. Errors stop a
run; warnings (code prefix W_) do not, but usually point at a modelling
mistake. `requires_run_length` tells you whether the model can drain on its
own -- if it is true and the run length is 0, a run will be refused.
name: validate_model

description:
Run (simulate) a model over its replications and return a COMPACT KPI digest -- never
the raw frames.

Validate first: a model with errors will not run. Every KPI comes back as a
mean with the half-width of its 95% confidence interval over replications;
a half-width near the mean means you need more replications; `run_to_precision`
finds how many. One replication gives no interval at all (null).

`bind_data=true` resolves the model's `series:` (time-series input) and
`orders` data bindings at RUN TIME, exactly as the UI/CLI's `--bind` does,
within this workspace's own network permission and file confinement --
there is no permission argument here, only whether to use it; a binding it
could not resolve is counted in "bindings" ({"problems", "first"}). Use
`resolve_data_bindings` first to preview what a binding would read.

The full frames stay in the workspace: page them out with `get_kpi_table`; kpi `log_level` is
faster.

"laws" are the operational-law checks and guardrails (utilisation, offered load, Little, flow
conservation, censoring, initial bias) -- warnings, never failures; a partial one names why
its numbers cannot be read at face value. Only when the model has them: "entities" (per
entity type, when there are several: Avg Time, Total Completed), "levels" (Average, Final,
Time Empty %, Time Full %), "queues" (per block: Balked, Reneged) and "agents" (per
population/state: Avg Count), in the same {mean, ci_half_width} form. "problems" is present
only when the run raised warnings while running (a part handed to nothing, a part leaving by
an exit its rule would not choose, a hold still open at the end): code, message, hint, block.

bind_data.description: Resolve series:/orders data bindings at run time first (default false), like the UI/CLI's `--bind`. This does NOT write bulk data into the model; it only affects this run.

log_level.description: kpi (summary frames), series (+ timeseries, dashboard), full (+ the three logs); study = kpi, explore and replay = full. Default explore, unless the model file sets its own. A frame left out gives E_NOT_RECORDED.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget; the run stops cleanly and returns what finished.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to run.

replications.description: Independent replications; defaults to the model's own setting.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units; defaults to the model's own setting.

seed.description: First replication's seed; replication r uses seed + r.

warmup.description: Warm-up time before statistics start; defaults to the model's own setting.

name: run_model

description:
Page through one results frame of the last `run_model` for this model.

Use it when the digest is not enough -- to see per-resource detail, the
per-entity log, or a time series. Ask for the smallest window you need:
`entity_log` and `timeseries` have thousands of rows.

frame.description: Which frame: system, resource_summary, entity_summary, user_summary, store_summary, entity_log, resource_log, store_log, timeseries, or any other name the run's `frames` lists (a conveyor line adds conveyor_flow, conveyor_zones, transfer_summary, route_holds, link_flow).

model.description: Workspace name of a model that has been run.

name: get_kpi_table

description:
Add or update a named scenario: a set of parameter overrides applied to
the base model before a run.

An override path addresses the layout by name, not by index -- for example
"resources.Server.capacity", "blocks.process_1.params.dist_params.rate" or
"simulation.replications". Scenarios are how you answer "A vs B, how sure
are we"; run them with `run_scenarios`.

description.description: Free-text note about what this scenario represents.

goal.description: The question this scenario answers, one sentence (max 500 characters).

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Scenario name; "Baseline" is implicit and always present.

name: upsert_scenario

description:
Run the model's scenarios (the options) and compare them against the baseline with
confidence intervals and a significance verdict: which option is better, and whether the
difference is significant.

This is the consultancy answer: for each KPI and scenario you get the
scenario's own mean with its CI, the DIFFERENCE against the baseline with
its own CI, and whether that difference interval excludes zero
("significant"). A non-significant difference means "not distinguishable at
this replication count", not "no difference".

"laws" are each scenario's law checks, {scenario: {"passed", "partial"}}, as run_model gives
them for one run: a partial law makes it not valid, no result to compare; censoring or
initial bias alone may bias it low, so a difference is not verified.

crn.description: Common random numbers (default true): pairs the scenarios so the comparison uses the low-variance paired-t interval.

kpis.description: KPI keys to report, e.g. ["system/Avg Throughput Time"]; omit for the system KPIs.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget for the whole sweep.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to run.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

scenarios.description: Scenario names to run; omit for all of them plus Baseline.

seed.description: Base seed; with CRN every scenario uses the same seeds.

name: run_scenarios

description:
Run the model's scenarios and price each against the baseline (is an option worth the
money?): extra capex, saving per year, payback, NPV and ROI over the `investment`
section's horizon, with confidence intervals from several replications.

A model without an `investment` section answers E_NO_INVESTMENT.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to run; it needs an `investment` section.

replications.description: Independent replications (capped at 200, like run_to_precision); defaults to the model's own setting.

seed.description: First replication's seed; replication r uses seed + r.

name: investment_case

description:
Keep adding replications until one KPI's confidence interval is narrow
enough (how sure the answer is), then report how many it took.

Use it instead of guessing a replication count: "how many runs do I need to
call this number to within 5%". If `met` comes back false, the cap or the
time budget was hit first and the reported half-width is what you actually
have.

absolute.description: Target half-width in the KPI's own units; overrides `relative`.

kpi.description: The KPI key to target, e.g. "system/Avg Throughput Time".

model.description: Workspace name of the model to run.

relative.description: Target half-width as a fraction of the mean (default 0.05 = 5%).

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

name: run_to_precision

description:
Run the model's Vensim-style reality checks: an input imposed on the
model (e.g. "workforce = 0") paired with a constraint expected to hold
given it (e.g. "then production = 0"). Each check is one deterministic
replication; a check with no violation passes.

"violation_time" and "snapshot" (the LEVEL/AUX/FLOW values at that instant) are null for a
check that passed; "note" is "" or a word on the outcome, such as an "eventually" check
that held from the start of its window.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget for the whole set of checks.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to run.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units; defaults to the model's own setting.

seed.description: Seed shared by every check's deterministic run (CRN across checks).

warmup.description: Warm-up time before statistics start; defaults to the model's own setting.

name: run_reality_checks

description:
Which feedback loop drives an SD model's behaviour, and when (Loops That
Matter, as in Stella). Runs the model once on its SD grid and scores every
loop at every step: a loop's relative score is its share of the change in
its stocks, signed (+ reinforcing, - balancing); the dominant loops at a
step are the fewest that explain at least half of it.

The *top* loops by |total|; a loop's "kind" is R/B from the run, U if its sign flips, D if
never active. Refused with E_LOOP_GRID without simulation.sd.

model.description: Workspace name of an SD model (needs simulation.sd).

run_length.description: Run length in base time units; defaults to the model's own setting.

seed.description: Seed of the one replication the analysis runs.

top.description: How many loops to return, strongest mean relative score first.

name: run_loop_dominance

description:
Estimate how much of the run to discard as warm-up, using MSER-5 on the
throughput-time series.

A steady-state model starts empty, which biases early observations low; the
warm-up is the time to reset statistics at. If `reliable` is false the run
was too short to tell -- lengthen it rather than trusting the number.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

replications.description: Replications to run for the estimate.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

name: suggest_warmup

description:
Search model parameters for the setting that minimises or maximises one KPI within a
replication budget, then confirm the winner statistically.

Every factor is an override path plus a range, exactly like a scenario
override but varying. The budget is a HARD cap on replications, so start
small (a few hundred) and raise it if `converged` is false. Constraints are
judged on confidence intervals, so a point may come back "unknown" rather
than feasible or infeasible. The best `confirm_top` points go through a
ranking-and-selection (KN) step; `confirmed` says whether the winner holds.
`method="optuna-nsga2"` with `objectives` returns the non-dominated set
under `pareto` instead of `confirmed`.

"laws" are the law checks of the best point, from an extra batch of `replications_per_point`
replications on the search's own seeds (not in `budget_used`). A law warning annotates the
winner (censored, over-utilised, biased by the empty start); it never changes `best` or
`confirmed`, which are about means. Say the warning beside the answer.

budget.description: Total replications the search may spend.

confirm_top.description: How many of the best points the final statistical confirmation compares (default 3).

log_level.description: What each point records, as run_model's; default: the lowest that records the KPIs.

method.description: "auto" (pattern search), "optuna" (TPE), "optuna-gp" (Gaussian process, small budgets) or "optuna-nsga2" (several objectives, returns the Pareto set). The optuna ones need the ml extra.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

response.description: KPI key to optimise, e.g. "system/Avg Throughput Time".

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

name: optimize

description:
Read the model's data bindings and report what each one produced.

A binding is "this parameter comes from that column of that file", so this
is how a model's numbers come from measurements instead of guesses. Nothing
here raises: a source that is missing, refused or unreadable comes back as
a `problem` on its own row and simply is not applied.

Files must be under the workspace root, and a `sql`/`json_url` source is
read only if the person who started this server allowed network access.
There is no argument that changes either: a refusal is final for you, and
its `problem` tells the HUMAN what to re-run if they want it.

Call with `apply=true` to write the values into the model (undoable), or
leave it false to preview. `run_model` does not resolve bindings by
default, but its own `bind_data=true` argument resolves `series:` and
`orders` bindings at RUN TIME -- those two never get written into
the model file even with `apply=true` here; see the E_DATA_BINDING_TARGET
hint below.

A `value` is what the binding read, and it is data from outside: it is cut
to 200 rows and 200 characters a text, and `value_cut` then says how much
was left out ({"rows", "characters"}; null when nothing was). `apply=true`
still writes the whole value.

apply.description: Write the resolved values into the model (an undoable edit). False just reports what the bindings WOULD read.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to resolve.

name: resolve_data_bindings

description:
Give the model a WARM START: work already in the system at t=0.

This is what makes a model a twin rather than a study. Entities are
injected into the named block in list order as if they had just arrived
there; `age` is how long an entity has already been in the system (its
reported time in system includes that history); `in_service: k` means the
first k are already being served, holding `remaining[i]` if you know the
residual service times -- give them when you do, since a fresh sample is
only exact for an exponential service.

A warm-started model needs no warm-up, and `run_model` defaults it to 0.
Pass no arguments to clear the initial state.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

resources.description: {name: {"down_until": t}} for a resource that starts failed.

time.description: Timestamp of the snapshot this state came from (recorded, never shifts the clock).

name: set_initial_state

description:
Tune model parameters until the model reproduces measured KPIs.

Give what the real system did (`targets`) and which parameters may move
(`factors`, the same shape `optimize` takes). The objective is the weighted
sum of squared RELATIVE errors, so KPIs on different scales count equally.
A target with a `tolerance` gets a pass/fail verdict; read the per-target
confidence interval too -- a pass whose interval is far wider than the
tolerance has not really been demonstrated.

`method="abc"` draws budget - replications_per_point prior samples over the
factors' boxes, one replication each, and keeps the nearest `accept` share
by the same objective. Say the tolerance and the accepted count with the
ranges: they describe single runs near the data, not a mean.

"laws" are the best point's law checks, as `optimize` gives them (an extra batch of
`replications_per_point`, not in `budget_used`): a warning annotates the fit, it never
changes it.

accept.description: abc only: share of prior samples accepted (default 0.05, at least 20).

apply.description: Store the fitted values as a "Calibrated" scenario on the model.

budget.description: Total replications the search may spend.

log_level.description: What each point records, as run_model's; default: the lowest that records the KPIs.

method.description: "optimize" (default): search for the best point. "abc": rejection ABC as well, a posterior range per factor.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to calibrate.

targets.description: [{"kpi", "observed", "weight"?, "tolerance"?}] -- the measured values the model must reproduce.

name: calibrate

description:
Forecast a short horizon from the model's CURRENT state, with
uncertainty bands and event probabilities.

Starts from the model's data bindings and initial state, runs a terminating
horizon with no warm-up, and answers "where is this heading". The band is
the empirical 5-95% range across replications -- where a single future run
is likely to land -- NOT a confidence interval of the mean, which is the
narrower `lb`/`ub` pair beside it.

An event's `kpi` may be any run KPI or a time-series peak,
`timeseries/<series>/max`, which is how you ask "was the queue EVER above
8" rather than "was it on average".

"laws" are the law checks of the forecast's own runs (no extra run); a warning says why a KPI
cannot be read at face value.

bind_data.description: Resolve the model's data bindings first (default true).

horizon.description: Run length in base time units -- a shift, a day.

kpis.description: KPI keys to report; omit for the curated system ones.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to forecast.

replications.description: Replications; a prediction band needs a few hundred to be stable.

name: forecast

description:
Fit candidate distributions to observed data and rank them, so a block's
duration comes from measurements instead of a guess.

Give either a file path under the workspace root or an inline list of
numbers. The ranking is by AIC (lower is better) with KS/AD statistics
alongside. Apply the winner by setting the block's `distribution` and
`dist_params` to the returned `spec`.

candidates.description: Distribution families to try; omit for all of them.

column.description: Column name in the file; defaults to the first numeric column.

path.description: CSV/TSV/XLSX file under the workspace root holding the sample.

top.description: How many ranked fits to return.

values.description: An inline list of numbers, instead of a file.

name: fit_distribution

description:
How much of each KPI's spread comes from the data its inputs were fitted to.

Each input's data is resampled with replacement and refitted in the family of its
best fit (an arrival schedule's timestamps are resampled by whole cycles), and the
model runs once for the fit to all the data and once per resample, all on the same
replication seeds, so resamples differ only in their inputs. Nothing is saved to the
model. The runs are (resamples + 1) x replications, at most 2000.

Per KPI: "run_ci", the 95% interval over the replications; "input_interval", the
interval with the inputs' uncertainty too (it always holds run_ci; a KPI the inputs
do not move keeps zero width); "input_share", the inputs' part of the variance of the
KPI's mean, the inputs' part being the variance of the resample means on common
random numbers (more replications shrink the rest, only more data shrinks it). The
intervals rest on "resamples_used" resamples, said in "notes"; a resample that could
not be refitted is counted in "failed" and left out.

With overrides (a change, as what_if takes it) each row is the change's difference
instead ("measure": "difference"): the baseline and the changed model run per resample on
the same seeds, so the interval is the difference's, not a level's. A later what_if on this
model quotes the latest answer in its "input_note".

inputs.description: One entry per input whose data is uncertain: {"path": a block's "...params.distribution" field, or "schedules.<name>.points" of an arrival schedule; "data": a CSV/TSV/XLSX file under the workspace root; "column": optional, the first numeric column by default; for a schedule also "bin_width" and "cycle" in base time units}.

kpis.description: KPI keys to report; default every system/ KPI.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

overrides.description: Optional change, as in what_if: every KPI row is then the changed model minus the baseline, both run per resample on the same seeds (twice the runs); nothing is saved to the model.

replications.description: Replications per resample (2 to 50); every resample runs on the same seeds.

resamples.description: Bootstrap resamples of the data (2 to 200).

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

seed.description: Base seed of the runs; the resampling has its own stream from it.

name: input_uncertainty

description:
Write the last run's results to a file: an Excel workbook, CSV folder,
a self-contained HTML report, or JSON.

Use `html` for the client-facing deliverable (it embeds the charts) and
`json` when another program will read the numbers. Run the model first.

format.description: Exporter name: xlsx, csv, html, json, or a plugin's own.

model.description: Workspace name of a model that has been run.

path.description: Destination under the workspace root (a directory for csv).

name: export

description:
Evaluate a built-in controller against a Policy-mode DECIDE.

Runs `episodes` episodes of `nagasim.rl.SimEnv`, driving every pending
decision at the named `policy` with `controller`. Use this to compare
"shortest" against "random" (or "roundrobin") before ever training
anything, or to sanity-check a model's Policy-mode DECIDE wiring.

episodes.description: Independent episodes to average over; episode i uses seed + i.

horizon.description: Episode length in base time units; the episode truncates there if the model has not drained first.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

policy.description: Decision-point name -- must match a Policy-mode DECIDE's `policy` param.

reward.description: "neg_wip", "throughput", "neg_time_in_system", or an expression string evaluated over model state at each decision (no `entity` in scope).

name: evaluate_policy

description:
Run a design of experiments and fit a response-surface surrogate over it
-- a fast stand-in for the simulation, for optimisation or
what-if exploration without spending more replications.

Every factor is swept per `design` and simulated `replications` times; the
surrogate is then fit on the point means, weighted by their precision.
Check `lack_of_fit` before trusting `suggest`-style extrapolation: it means
the model misses structure the replication noise does not explain, so
"quadratic" or "auto" (or "gp"/"forest" with scikit-learn) may do better
than "linear".

With `confirm_top` N, the surface's best N distinct points are simulated and compared
by KN (as `optimize` confirms its winner): the surface proposes, the runs decide. It is
refused when `lack_of_fit` is true ("confirm_refused" says why), since that surface's
ranking is not worth runs. The confirmed winner carries its "laws", as optimize's does.

With confirm_top, "confirmed" (or null) and "confirm_refused" (text or null) are added.

confirm_top.description: Confirm the surface's best N suggestions by simulation (KN ranking and selection on common random numbers); 0 (default) fits only. Refused when the surface shows lack of fit.

design.description: full[:levels] (default full:2), lhs:<n>, or oat -- same grammar as `naga doe --design`.

factors.description: [{"path": "resources.Server.capacity", "kind": "integer", "low": 1, "high": 5}], same shape as the `optimize` tool's factors.

goal.description: "min" or "max": the direction the suggestions and their confirmation look for (with confirm_top).

kind.description: "linear", "quadratic", "auto" (picks by CV RMSE), or -- only if scikit-learn is installed -- "gp"/"forest".

log_level.description: What each point records, as run_model's; default: the lowest that records the KPIs.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget for the whole design and its confirmation.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

response.description: KPI key to fit a surface for, e.g. "system/Avg Throughput Time".

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

name: fit_surrogate

description:
Undo the last edit to a model: take back what was just added, changed or removed.

Every tool that changes a model pushes exactly one undo entry, so one
`undo` reverses one tool call. Use it to back out an edit whose returned
problems show it was wrong.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

name: undo

description:
Redo the edit that `undo` reversed.

Only available while nothing new has been edited since the undo: any fresh
mutation clears the redo stack, exactly like the editor.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

name: redo

description:
Run one replication of a model under a debugger: start it, or continue it,
until a stop, one step, a model time, a pending decision or the end. Use it to explain
behaviour, such as why a queue grows or where entities get stuck.

The run is kept between calls, one per model, so the usual loop is: set stops
and watches, call again and again, and read `debug_inspect` whenever it
returns. A stop fires on a change -- an entity entering a block, an expression
going from false to true -- so calling again always moves on. Nothing here
changes the results: a run that is stopped, stepped and inspected ends with the
same numbers as `run_model` with one replication and the same seed.

`back` undoes the previous call's move: the run is rebuilt where that call
found it, by replaying the same seed and decisions, so nothing is approximated.

`state` says why it returned: "back", "stop" (see `hits`), "step", "time" (reached
`to`), "decision" (a Policy DECIDE waits: answer with `decisions`; the clock
cannot move until you do), "budget" (max_seconds ran out; call again),
"horizon" or "drained" (the run is over; `restart` to debug again). `hits`
lists every stop that fired during the call and is read at every return, so
it can be non-empty beside any state, not only "stop".

A call is refused (E_BAD_ARGUMENT) before anything changes when `stops` or
`watches` is not a list, has more than 50 entries or holds a text of more than
500 characters, or `to` is not a finite number; a bad stop likewise
(E_BAD_STOP). Then a start or `restart` happens (with the new stops and watches,
if given), then `decisions` are applied, then on a continuing run the new stops
and watches take effect, then the run moves. A refused
decision answers with an error before the run moves: a continuing run keeps its
stops and watches as they were, but the decisions listed before the refused one
stay applied. A start or `restart` is not undone by a later error in the same
call.

back.description: True: go back to where the previous call left the run, exactly (it is replayed from the seed and the decisions made), and return without moving. The replay runs from t = 0 within max_seconds; when it does not fit, E_BUDGET and the run stays where it was. Not with `to`, `step`, `scope`, `decisions` or `restart`.

decisions.description: Answers to pending decisions: [{"policy", "option", "request_id"}] (request_id optional: the policy's oldest). Applied after the checks of the other arguments and after a start or `restart`, before the run moves.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget for this call; the run stays where it got to. 0 means no budget: the call runs until a stop, `to`, a decision or the end.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to debug.

restart.description: True: drop the run and start again from t = 0 on the model as it is now, keeping the stops and watches unless new ones are given.

scope.description: With `step`: a submodel instance (or a block); the step goes on to the next event of a block inside it, so it stays where you are looking.

seed.description: Seed of the run; read only when the run starts or restarts.

step.description: True: stop at the next event the trace shows (one entity move, one resource change).

stops.description: Replaces the stops (a list of at most 50, each text at most 500 characters): [{"block": name}] stops when an entity enters that block (a submodel instance name: anything inside it), [{"entity": id}] when that entity is created or moves, [{"expr": text}] when the expression becomes true. A block or entity stop may add "entity" (that entity only) and "when" (an expression read with the entering entity, e.g. 'entity.e_type == "Red"'). Omit to keep them, [] to clear.

to.description: Model time to run to at most (a finite number); omit for no time limit.

watches.description: Replaces the watch expressions, read at every return (a list of at most 50 texts of at most 500 characters). Omit to keep, [] to clear.

name: debug_run

description:
Read the state of a model's debug run where it stands, without moving it.

Call it after `debug_run` returns. With no argument it is the overview: how
many entities sit in each block, every resource's state, every level's value
and the decisions waiting. `block` adds that block's queue and entities;
`entity` adds one live entity's attributes, the model's own included.

Counts are per block of the top level: a block inside a submodel instance is
counted with its instance, and `block` then answers for the instance (see the
"name" it returns).

With `block`: "block": {"name", "count", "in_service", "queue": [entity ids waiting, oldest
first], "entities": [ids]} (50 ids at most each); with `entity`: "entity": {"id", "type",
"created", "attributes"}, or null once it is disposed or inside a batch.

block.description: A block or submodel instance to look into; omit for the overview only.

entity.description: Id of an entity to read (from a hit, a queue or `pending`).

model.description: Workspace name of a model with a debug run.

name: debug_inspect

description:
Run a model once, on one seed, and list what happened in it that no KPI reports,
as facts with numbers: blocks no entity entered, resources never seized (never used), resources
with a unit doing no work (free, or held by an entity waiting elsewhere) while
entities waited for them, and entities still in the model at the end. Use it after
building or changing a model to find mistakes a run does not fail on, such as a
branch never taken, a wrong resource name, a multi-resource seize in the wrong
order or a HOLD never released.

A fact says what was measured and what can cause it, never that the model is
wrong: some facts are what the model intends. The run is the one `run_model` makes
with one replication and the same seed; nothing is kept.

Kinds come in this order: never_entered, never_seized, idle_while_waiting, left_waiting and
truncated (the trace hit its cap, so the facts cover the run only up to `t`); at most 20 of
each, then one fact saying how many more there are.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to run.

run_length.description: Model time to run to; omit for the model's own run length.

name: run_facts

description:
Check a plant mapping against a model and, given a recorded plant log,
say what the plant looked like at the log's last instant.

A plant mapping says what each key a plant sends asserts about the model
(which block an item is in, how many units of a resource are busy, what a
level holds). The log's observations become the same trace events a run
emits, so `blocks` and `resources` read exactly like a run's playback.

Both files are data under the workspace root. This tool opens no
connection and has no argument that could: watching a live plant is the
person's own `naga plant watch` with their connections file.

`counts` says what was dropped, repaired or made up, by reason; `problems`
carries the mapping's errors (then nothing is replayed) and the replay's
warnings.

With a log, the answer adds the plant's state at the log's last instant.

log.description: Recorded plant log (one JSON object a line, as `naga watch --record` writes), a path relative to the workspace root. Empty: only check the mapping.

mapping.description: Plant mapping (*.plantmap.json), a path relative to the workspace root.

model.description: Workspace name of the model the mapping is for.

name: get_plant_timeline

description:
What the plant looks like now, as the running twin last wrote it.

A twin is started by a person (`naga twin run`), reads their plant through
their connections and writes a result every few seconds; this tool reads
that result and nothing else. `sources` says whether each source is live
and how old its last word is; `view` holds the items in each block, each
resource's state and the levels at model time `at` (`approximate` is true
when the plant names no items, so counts are estimates; `counters` is what
the plant itself counted as having left a block since the twin first saw
that counter, observed and not estimated); `problems` are
coded, with what the twin did about each. Check `written` before trusting
the picture: a twin that stopped leaves its last result behind, and one
that runs writes every `cadence.every` seconds (null: it is run one step
at a time by a scheduler). `at` is model time, in `model.time_unit` from
`model.epoch` (null where the source has no epoch).
name: get_twin_monitor

description:
The running twin's latest forecast, and how its earlier ones compare
with what the plant then did.

`forecast.status` is "ok", "running", "skipped" (a source is down),
"refused" (the model cannot be started from the plant's state: `reason`
and the monitor's problems say which kind), "failed" or "none"; with any
status but "ok" the record shown is the last good one. The record names
what it was computed from (`state` and `model` hashes, `seed`, `from`,
`horizon`, `replications`), so it can be reproduced; `finished` and `took`
(seconds) say when it could first be read and how long it ran. `kpis` are
end-of-horizon means with a confidence interval (`lb`, `ub`) and the 5-95%
band of single replications; `points` are predictions at stated times.
`comparison` sets each prediction whose time has come beside the observed
value: `inside` says whether it fell in the 5-95% band. `approximate` is
about counts of items inferred where the plant names none (`system/WIP`
then rests on estimates); a `block/<name>/out` row is what the plant's own
counter counted and is observed either way. `scores` sums those
comparisons by series and lead (how far ahead, in model time): `coverage`
is the share inside the band (`nominal`, 0.9, when the model is right; a
row with `whole` true holds whole numbers only and covers more than that
on a right model, so compare its `pinball`), `bias` the mean of observed
minus forecast mean, `error` the mean absolute error, `pinball` the
quantile loss of the band (lower is better). Never quote a row without
`basis` (forecasts, points, `missed` because the twin was late or a source
not ready, `lost` because a counter lost count, since when; `same_seed`
forecasts are not independent samples), and say `reason` when there are no
rows. Readings overlap in time: this is evidence in distribution, not a
test. When `forecast.actions` is there, the forecast ASSUMES actions a
person took through the twin's outbox are in the plant (`assumes` says so
in words; `get_twin_recommendations` lists them under `standing`): say so
whenever you quote such a forecast.
name: get_twin_forecast

description:
What the running twin recommends now (what we should do), and what became of
its earlier advice. Read-only: this tool cannot deliver, approve, reject
or address a recommendation, and no tool can.

The person who started the twin gave it candidate actions and one KPI
(`kpi`, with `better`: "higher" or "lower"). After each forecast the twin
runs every candidate from the same plant state on the same random numbers
(`crn`) and sets it beside doing nothing. An item has its `action`
({"verb", "target", "value"}), `baseline` and `with_action` (means of the
KPI), `effect` (the mean difference) with its 95% interval (`low`, `high`),
`confidence` (the share of replications in which the action did better)
and a `verdict`: "better" (the interval excludes no effect), "no_effect"
(it includes it: do not present this as a gain), "worse", "failed" or
"standing" (already taken). Only "better" items have a `rank`, an `id` and
a `status`: "proposed" (shown, not delivered), "delivered" (written to the
person's own outbox, unanswered), "taken", "rejected", "expired" or
"dropped". With `status` "none", say `reason`: "no_forecast" (a source is
down or the state was refused: see `get_twin_forecast`), "none_better",
"kpi", "replications" or "failed". `standing` lists the actions a person
took, which every later forecast now assumes until a person ends one
(`ended` lists those). `effects` is what the plant's
own counter then showed over one horizon (`observed`), and whether that fell
in the 5-95% band the twin gave (`inside_interval`); "missed", "lost" and
"not_observable" say why there is no number. This is what the model says,
in distribution: not a causal claim about the plant, and one effect outside
its band proves little. A proposal is acted on by a person, in their own
queue or in the editor; if asked to approve or send one, say that you
cannot.

Keep a source of the study in its inputs/ folder: copy a workspace file, or store text
(a call transcript, notes). Then name it with study_update(changes={"sources": [{"id",
"text", "input": <the returned path>}]}) so the inputs step can check it.

description:
Test one model step: write the whole model, run it, check it, and store it as a new
version (or as a draft when it fails). Send the complete model file as `layout`, or `model`
(the name of a model open in the workspace), or `patch` (changes to the
last version), and a one-line note. A model that does not validate or run is stored as a
draft with its problems, not refused: read "problems", fix the model, step again.

The replications come from a precision target, not from the model's own
simulation.replications: a first pass of 10, then, if a goal KPI's 95% confidence interval is
wider than its target, one rerun (same seed) with the count the widest needs, up to the size's
cap (quick 50, standard 200, deep 1000). The target is a relative half-width (quick 10%,
standard 5%, deep 2%; set another with study_update precision={"relative": 0.03}) or an
absolute one per goal ("precision": 0.5 in the KPI's unit). With no goal KPI the count is 10
and provisional. A cap reached makes the "precision" check partial, never failed.

The model's "scenarios" (a list of {"name", "overrides": [{"path":
"resources.<name>.capacity", "value": 2}]}) run with the step, with the same replications
and seed, up to the size's cap; their goal KPIs and goals met come back in "scenarios".

`changes` (the same keys and shapes as study_update) is recorded first, in the same call, so
a step that also records the goals or a validation needs one call, not two. Scenario
overrides sent as {"resources.<name>.capacity": 2} are mapped to the list shape; a target
component without blocks whose name matches a block name is mapped to it. Both are listed in
"normalised". Example: study_step(study="naga-studies/cranes", layout={...the whole model...},
note="add the second crane", changes={"assumptions": [{"id": "a1", "text": "...", "source": "..."}]}).

A tail goal {"id", "text", "kpi": "<resource>/Time in Queue", "share_above": 15, "high": 0.05}
bounds the share of entities that waited over 15 at that resource (FIFO only), stored per
replication as the KPI "<resource>/Share waiting over 15"; "kpi": "Total Wait" sums each
entity's waits over every queue ("Share with total wait over 15"). Either is judged, sized and
compared like any KPI; when it cannot be computed it stays not_verified and "tail_note" says why.

A version has no report file by default (the answer is the light output); study_report
writes it on request. With scenarios: "scenarios": {name: {"kpis": {goal KPI: {mean,
ci_half_width}}, "goals": {goal id: met|not_met|not_verified}}}, and "scenario_error" or
"scenarios_skipped" when a run failed or the cap cut some; "normalised" when an input was
mapped. A scenario whose law checks warn carries "laws": {"passed", "partial"} and a partial
"scenario <name>" check says why. A partial law: not valid, goals not_verified, why in place
of its numbers. Censoring or initial bias only: a goal a low bias may flip is not_verified.

changes.description: Keys to record in the same call, with the shapes of study_update's changes. Recorded before the step.

model.description: Instead of layout: the name of a model open in the workspace, stepped as it is.

note.description: One line: what changed in this step and why.

patch.description: Instead of layout: [{"path", "value"}] changes to the last version, in the scenario override form, e.g. [{"path": "resources.Server.capacity", "value": 2}].

description:
Check the last model version against a textbook answer and record the validation.

kind="queue_formula" applies when the model is one arrival stream (exponential interarrival
times) feeding one FIFO resource: the engine runs the model 100 times longer than its own
run length (warm-up 10% of that, 10 replications, seed 0), compares the mean wait in queue
with M/M/c (Erlang C) or M/G/1 (Pollaczek-Khinchine) and records a known_answer validation
that passes within 5% relative error. Any other model answers E_STUDY_NOT_APPLICABLE with the
reason, so the person is asked for another validation.
Example: study_validate(study="naga-studies/cranes").

"model" and "formula" are the simulated and the formula's mean wait, "rel_error" their
relative difference and "passed" whether it is within 5%.

kind.description: The known answer to check against; only queue_formula (M/M/c or M/G/1) exists.

study.description: Study folder relative to the workspace root (the id study_start returned).

name: study_validate

description:
Vary one assumption at a time (arrival and service parameters, capacities) around a version,
with common random numbers and the version's stored replications and seed, and rank them by
how much each moves the goal KPIs. Answers {"file", "ranked": [{path, label, swing}],
"changes_answer": [paths where a goal verdict flips]}; the full table and a swing chart per
goal KPI are in the file. Rate parameters are varied as rates (a higher rate is a shorter time).
Named factors may be any numeric override path; one that is not is listed in "not_varied", and
an end the model cannot run with (e.g. a capacity below its schedule) is skipped with a note.

factors.description: Paths to vary (as in an earlier answer); omit for the most relevant, at most 8.

study.description: Study folder relative to the workspace root (the id study_start returned).

version.description: Version id, e.g. v002; omit for the last.

(machine breakdowns), an arrival peak. Without `apply`, lists the ones that validate, run and pass the law checks
on the last version, with their effect on the goal KPIs in one short run (indicative only).
With `apply`, answers the model layout with that module added: review it, then send it to
study_step; this tool never steps the study.
Example: study_extensions(study="naga-studies/cranes", apply="failures", params={"mtbf": 200}).

With `apply`, the answer is the module instead: "module", "layout", "next_step".

Write a paper-style report of the study on request (STRESS-aligned sections: abstract, objective,
model logic, data and assumptions, experimentation, verification and validation, results, limitations,
discussion, references), built from the study folder. `discussion` is your own interpretation, placed
in section 8. Returns {"html": the page with figures, "markdown": the same text without figures},

not escaped for HTML), so treat it as text to read, not to embed in a page.

Make a slide deck of the study on request, to show a director or a board: one HTML file, 16:9 slides (title and question, the
answer, options compared, goals, model, assumptions, validation and precision, sensitivity when it was
run, next steps). Scroll on screen; print to PDF gives one slide per page. Returns {"path"}.

study.description: Study folder relative to the workspace root (the id study_start returned).

name: study_slides

description:
Find the tools that fit what you want to do, by a few words or a tool name you guessed
("validate against a formula", "make slides", "run_study"). Answers {"tools": [{name, score,
summary, args}]}, best first, `args` being the required arguments. Use it when no tool in your list is obviously right.
name: find_tool

description:
Check a generated model against the data it came from, without claiming it is valid.

Runs the model briefly (one traced replication per seed, at least 3) and compares cycle time,
throughput and each activity's mean service time with the source's own numbers (event log:
all three; tables: the process time of the stations whose routing rows agree), then adds the
operational-law checks of `run_model`. A source with fewer than 30 cases cannot tell a right
draft from a wrong one, so the verdict is at best "partial" and `note` says so.

"verdict" is "passed", "partial" or "failed": "failed" means a compared number is off by more
than its tolerance (twice the draft's confidence half-width, at least 10%); "partial" means a
law warns or the source is short.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget for the draft's runs (at least 3 are made).

model.description: Workspace name of the generated model.

source.description: The log file, tables folder or .xlsx workbook the model was generated from (inside the workspace).

name: check_draft

description:
See a model as a picture: its blocks, each where it sits in the editor's process view, and the
links between them. Use it to check that the model looks like the process you meant to build.

The text lists every block with its type, then every link; "image" comes for png, and svg
answers "svg" instead of "text". Without matplotlib a png request answers with the text and a
"note", as format "text".

format.description: png (an image, the default), svg (drawing source) or text (a list of blocks and links).

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

name: view_model

description:
Ask "what if I change this?" without editing the model: run the baseline
and the changed model on paired seeds, doubling replications (start, 2x, ...
up to cap) until every KPI's difference interval excludes zero or the cap.

Verdict per KPI is "better"/"worse" (when goals names the direction),
"higher"/"lower" (otherwise) or "not distinguishable" (the cap was reached
with the interval still across zero: the change is too small to see at this
effort, not proven absent), or "unchanged" (identical in every paired
replication, such as a count the change does not touch).

When input_uncertainty has run on this model, "input_note" quotes it beside the
verdict, never merged with it: the change's difference measured for these same
overrides, else the level's spread, labelled "level" (a level's spread is not the
difference's). No note when nothing was measured.

goals.description: Optional {kpi: "min" | "max"}: with it the verdict reads better/worse.

kpis.description: KPI keys to judge; omit for the system KPIs.

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

overrides.description: Scenario-style overrides, e.g. [{"path": "resources.Server.capacity", "value": 2}]; nothing is saved to the model.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

start.description: First replication count (doubles until the answer is clear).

name: what_if

description:
What makes up a KPI, in one call: its contributors, ranked, each a measured number
with its 95% interval, plus one suggested what_if test of the top one (never run).

Time KPIs (and WIP, by Little's law): per resource, the wait a completed entity spent
there, and the rest as "processing and moving"; "coverage" says how much of the KPI the
waits add up to. Throughput: per resource its bottleneck share (when the model collects
it, outputs.bottleneck) or else its usage, with down and blocked beside. A resource KPI:
that resource's usage, down, blocked and wait. With overrides: the same rows for the
baseline and the changed model, ranked by the paired difference, each with a verdict
("higher", "lower", "not distinguishable", "unchanged").

A ranking says how the KPI is made up, not why: every row is labelled "measured", and
the suggested test is how to check the top row -- pass its "arguments" to what_if to
spend that run.

"factors" is a hypothesis to search, not a finding: the capacities of the top resource
rows that hold 95% of the rows (integer, from one below to two above the current value),
then the sensitivity paths that change the answer, at most 4; pass it to optimize as
`factors` unchanged. "factors_from" says where each one came from.

cap.description: Most replications to try with overrides.

kpi.description: The KPI to explain: "system/Avg Throughput Time", "system/Avg WIP", "system/Avg WIP (Little)", "system/Throughput (per time unit)" or one resource's "resource/<name>/<metric>".

model.description: Workspace name of the model.

overrides.description: Optional scenario-style overrides, as in what_if: with them the rows compare the baseline and the changed model on paired seeds; nothing is saved to the model.

replications.description: Replications of the one batch; with overrides the first count, doubled until the KPI's difference is clear.

run_length.description: Run length in base time units.

sensitivity.description: Optional study_sensitivity answer (or its sensitivity.json): its changes_answer paths join the factors for optimize.

name: explain_kpi

description:
The open-and-run gate: does the model open in the editor with NO errors, using the
plugins this person enabled, and run one replication? Call it before you say a model you
built or edited is done; a model that fails it is not done.

"status" is "pass", "fail" or "stopped" (the budget ran out: it opens with no errors but the
run was not finished); the message says what failed first (an error in the Problems panel,
with its fix, or the exception of the run). A block type that "comes from a plugin that is not
loaded" needs the person to trust its folder in Settings > Plugins; `propose_plugin_folder` can
only suggest one.

max_seconds.description: Wall-clock budget for the run; a run it stops answers status "stopped", neither a pass nor a fail.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to check.

name: check_model_opens

description:
Propose a plugin folder for the person to trust. It is added to their Settings > Plugins
list SWITCHED OFF and marked "added by assistant": nothing in it runs until the person ticks
it there. Only a folder inside this workspace can be proposed; a folder already listed is
left exactly as it is. Tell the person to open Settings > Plugins and enable it.

"state" is "proposed" (added, off), or "listed" (already there, with "enabled" saying
whether the person turned it on).

folder.description: The plugin folder, inside the workspace (relative to its root, or absolute under it).

model.description: Workspace name of the model that needs the plugin.

name: propose_plugin_folder

description:
Translate a system-dynamics file into a new model: Stella/iThink XMILE (.xmile, .stmx) or
Vensim (.mdl), by the file's extension.

Reads stocks, flows, auxiliaries, lookups (as lookup tables) and dimensions or subscript
ranges (as subscripts) with a small stdlib reader (no `pysd`), into the workspace under
*name*, exactly like `open_model` does for a model JSON file. The file must be under the
workspace root -- a path that escapes it is refused, and there is no argument that widens that.

A construct this cannot translate (a module or macro, external data, a conveyor/queue
stock, a dimension mapping or subscript equivalence, an unknown function or name) is
reported in `import_problems` (code `E_SDIMPORT_UNSUPPORTED`) and left out of the model
rather than guessed at; an approximation (a bare DELAY, a non-euler/rk4 method, ...) is
`W_SDIMPORT_APPROX`. "errors", "warnings" and "problems" are the usual model-validation
answer, over what DID translate.

name.description: Workspace name to load it under; defaults to the file stem.

path.description: Stella/iThink XMILE (.xmile/.stmx) or Vensim (.mdl) file, relative to the workspace root.

name: import_sd_model

description:
One layer of equal items on a pallet, as the slots of a pallet pattern.

"column" is the better of the two plain grids; "block" splits the pallet once and
turns the items 90 degrees in one part, which packs more when neither grid fills
it; "best" keeps the layout with the most items. Each slot is an item's centre
from the pallet's centre (x along the pallet's length) and its rotation in
degrees. It writes nothing: put the slots under a record's `layers` (for example
as layer "A", stacked [{"layer": "A"}, {"layer": "A", "transform": "rotate180"}])
and store it with upsert_record in "pallet_patterns".

item_length.description: The item's length, in the same unit.

item_width.description: The item's width, in the same unit.

kind.description: "column", "block" or "best" (default): the layout with the most items.

overhang.description: How far an item may pass the pallet's edge (default 0).

pallet_length.description: The pallet's length, in the model's length unit.

pallet_width.description: The pallet's width, in the same unit.

description:
Add one belt piece on the floor plan: a CONVEYOR whose `path` is *segments*, starting at
(x, y) and travelling at *rotation*.

With *snap_to* ("A.out", "A.d0", or a transfer exit "X.left") the piece starts at that
port, facing its way, and a link with `source_port` / `target_port` is added, so no
coordinates are computed by hand. One undo entry. Segment lengths and radii are in the
model's length unit.

model.description: Workspace name of the model to edit.

name.description: Name of the new belt piece.

rotation.description: Direction of travel at the entry, degrees clockwise on screen (0 east, 90 south), like set_layout; ignored with snap_to.

segments.description: The belt's pieces, entry to end (the CONVEYOR `path` param): {"straight": length} or {"arc": {"radius": r, "angle": degrees, "turn": "left"|"right"}}.

snap_to.description: "<block>.<port>" of a belt or transfer exit ("A.out", "A.d0", "X.left"): the piece starts at that port, facing its way, and the two are linked.

speed.description: Belt speed, model length per time unit; default: the type's datasheet speed (untyped: block default).

type.description: Conveyor type: "" (untyped), "belt", "roller", "chain", "pallet" or "mdr". A typed piece gets the type's datasheet speed in its params.

x.description: Floor-plan x of the belt's entry, in metres; ignored with snap_to.

y.description: Floor-plan y (south is +y), in metres; ignored with snap_to.

name: place_piece

description:
Add a CONVEYOR_TRANSFER (moves each load onto one of its exits) on the floor plan, in one
undo entry.

Its exits are ports: `place_piece` the belt that takes each with snap_to "<module>.<exit>",
